title: Hiring for Potential or Experience? Look at the Evidence First
summary: Years of experience predict job performance only weakly. How to weigh potential against experience using real evidence, the team's next year and the coaching you have.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Two finalists for one backend role. Candidate A has six years on your exact stack and has run the kind of migration you're about to start. Candidate B has two years on a different stack, but the interview notes keep coming back to one moment: the interviewer dropped a hint, B picked it up, rethought the design and finished with a better answer than they started with.

The debrief splits. Half the room says A is the safe pick. The other half says B will be better in a year. Both sides are guessing, and both are guessing from labels.

What years of experience actually predict

Experience feels safe because you can see it. It's on the CV, it comes with numbers, and the stories sound close to the work in front of you. The research is less impressed. A 2019 meta-analysis pooled 81 samples and found that pre-hire work experience had a corrected correlation of .06 with job performance and .00 with turnover (Van Iddekinge et al., Personnel Psychology, 2019). Experience predicted a bit better for people who had just started the new job, and the authors caution employers against selecting on these experience measures unless more positive evidence turns up.

Experience still counts for something. The point is that a count of years is a weak stand-in for what you actually want, which is judgment. Six years can be six years of growth, or one year repeated six times. The number can't tell you which.

Both need evidence

Experience and potential aren't opposites. Both are claims, and both need proof you saw with your own eyes in the interview.

  • Experience should show up as judgment: clear trade-offs, a feel for where things break, debugging that starts from the likeliest cause, and the sense to spot a familiar pattern without forcing every problem into it.
  • Potential should show up as learning behavior: how someone takes a hint, drops a wrong assumption, asks for missing context and folds a new constraint into a better answer.

A senior candidate can have long exposure and little growth. A junior one can have short exposure and a fast learning loop. So skip "who has the better history?" Ask "what did we actually see that tells us this person can do the work this team needs over the next year?"

Start from the team's next year

The same candidate can be a great hire for one team and a hard one for another. If you're about to run a fragile migration and nobody is free to supervise, direct experience may be the responsible choice. Someone who has seen those failure modes before cuts risk fast. If the team already has enough seniors but lacks careful executors or future tech leads, hiring for potential may be the better long-term bet.

Before you compare candidates, write down two things: the work coming in the next six to twelve months, and how much coaching time the team can honestly give. Most potential-versus-experience debates get easier once those two lines are on the table.

Potential has a cost

Someone with less experience needs more onboarding, clearer feedback, smaller first tasks and a lead who actually makes time to coach. If a team says it hires for potential but has no patience for questions, no review habit and no room for small mistakes caught early, it isn't really hiring for potential. It's asking someone to grow in poor soil and calling the risk theirs.

Say the cost out loud in the debrief: "B will need someone to pair with most days for the first month. Who's doing that?" If nobody can answer, the honest pick may be A, at least for this opening.

So does experience

Someone who has done the job many times brings useful shortcuts. They can also bring assumptions from a different company, scale or culture, and past success can harden into a script. Don't punish experience for that. Check whether the person still listens, adapts and learns your system before reaching for the fix that worked last time.

Design the interview to show both

"High potential" and "very experienced" are conclusions. The interview's job is to collect the evidence underneath them, and structure helps a lot. A 2022 re-analysis of decades of personnel selection research ranked structured interviews as the top selection procedure for predicting job performance, with a mean operational validity of .42 (Sackett, Zhang, Berry and Lievens, Journal of Applied Psychology, 2022). Google's re:Work guide shows how to set one up: the same kinds of questions for everyone in the role, and a rubric written in advance for what poor, borderline, solid and outstanding answers cover (re:Work: A guide to structured interviewing). When I rebuilt the hiring loop for an 11-person team, structured interviews were part of it.

A few prompts that show both sides:

  • Learning: halfway through a design problem, give a hint. What changes in their answer?
  • Judgment: "Tell me about a trade-off you got wrong. What do you watch for now?"
  • Adapting: move a constraint mid-problem ("now it has to work offline") and see how they rework the plan.
  • Knowing their limits: "Which part of this would you want a second pair of eyes on?"

The most useful evidence often shows up in the correction, after the first answer.

Build a mix

Be wary of rules that sound too clean: only seniors, only hungry juniors, only people from big tech. They cut uncertainty, and they cut attention along with it. Healthy teams are a mix of people who have walked the road before, people ready to stretch, people who keep quality steady and people who ask fresh questions about habits that have gone on autopilot. If your team leans hard to one side, that's useful input for the next hire. It's also one more reason to stop letting "culture fit" decide it.

Before the next debrief

  • Put the next six to twelve months of work, and the coaching time you really have, at the top of the hiring doc.
  • Swap "experienced" and "high potential" on the scorecard for the behaviors you expect to see.
  • Add one hint-and-adapt moment to your technical interview.
  • If you pick potential, name the person who will coach and put the time on their calendar.

faqs.q: Does years of experience predict job performance?
faqs.a: Only weakly. A 2019 meta-analysis by Van Iddekinge and colleagues, pooling 81 samples, found a corrected correlation of .06 between pre-hire experience and job performance and .00 with turnover. Experience is more useful when you look for the judgment it should have built.

faqs.q: When should a team hire for experience?
faqs.a: When the work ahead is high-risk and nobody has time to coach, such as a fragile migration. Someone who has seen the same failure modes can cut risk quickly.

faqs.q: When does hiring for potential make sense?
faqs.a: When the team has seniors with real time to coach, review habits that catch mistakes early, and a need for future leads or careful executors. Without that support, hiring for potential mostly moves the risk onto the new hire.

faqs.q: How can an interview show potential?
faqs.a: Use a structured interview and watch how candidates use a hint, handle a changed constraint and talk about a trade-off they got wrong. A 2022 re-analysis by Sackett and colleagues ranked structured interviews as the top selection procedure for predicting job performance.
